newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Yachting-Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.
newsitem.headline: Australian Yachting-Peter Campbell's Rhumbline Column.

text.p: By Peter Campbell*
SYDNEY TO HOBART 1996 - BETTER THAN THE FILM !

Race line honours favourite Morning Glory breaks US$300,000 carbon fibre mast...Jumbo air freighter aircraft diverted to carry 36-metre tall spare across the Tasman from Auckland...just beats night curfew...Crew works all night to assemble and step replacement rig...fleet hit by 40-knot southerly buster only hours after start...Main rival for line honours breaks mast... Winds swing to north and Morning Glory surfs across Bass Strait.
And, in nail-biting night sail across Storm Bay and up the Derwent River Morning Glory breaks the 21-year-old race record by 29 minutes.

As media director for the Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart Yacht Race, I could not have written a better script for the 52nd annual race down the Australian east coast, across Bass Strait and down Tasmania's east coast for the often frustrating sail up the River Derwent to the finish line off historic Battery Point.
Back in 1975, I was out on the Derwent as Kialoa sailed up to set the record that was to stand unbeaten for longer than any major ocean race in the world.
It was an inspiring sight as the beautiful US maxi ketch swept up the river.
This year, it was an awesome sight as Morning Glory took line honours and finally broke the record.
Looking down the river the 80-footer appeared to be sailing out of small village of lights as some 200 spectator craft tried to keep pace with her.
At times, with the westerly wind gusting up to 20 knots, she was powering upwind at 12 to 15 knots and crossed the line with just 29 minutes to spare.

The dockside welcome 30 minutes later was overwhelming for Morning Glory's owner, German industrialist HASSO PLATTNER as he collected the $300,000 cheque from Telstra's MICHAEL ROSE when the yacht came alongside the dock shortly before 4 a.m.
With the crowd ten-deep, champagne flowing, the elation was even greater when he announced he would share the rich prize with the crew of 21.

"The Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart is undoubtedly one of the great ocean races of the world, but I have also never experienced such a welcome at the finish," said PLATTNER, who is the co-founder of SAP, the world's fourth-largest computer software company.
NO APPEAL LODGED AS YET BY BZW CHALLENGE

While the 1996 Telstra Sydney-to-Hobart is all over, with the arrival just after midnight on Friday of the last yacht, the 34-footer David Hannah from Adelaide and mid-morning dockside presentation to the skipper, 25-year-old CATHERINE JONES, a cloud still hangs over the overall International Measurement System (IMS) result.

The Cruising Yacht Club of Australia (CYCA) has announced the winner as Ausmaid, the Farr-47 owned and skippered by Italian-born, Melbourne-based businessman GIORGIO GJERGJA, with Exile, WARWICK MILLER-s Reichel/Pugh-66 from the Royal Kong Yacht Club, second overall and Atara, the Farr-43 skippered by ROGER HICKMAN from the CYCA, in third place.
In fourth place was the newly imported Farr-designed Corel-45, BZW Challenge, skippered by RAY ROBERTS.

However, ROBERTS has indicated he will lodge an appeal with the Australian Yachting Federation (AYF) against the redress granted by the race jury for time lost when the yacht diverted to search an area in which a flare had been sighted on the second night at sea.

ROBERTS had sought two hours redress but the jury granted him 33 minutes. This made no change to the top four placings overall, but had the two hours been granted it could have upset second and possibly first place.
ROBERTS has two weeks to lodge an appeal with the AYF.
COMPUTER PROBLEMS UPSET COFFS HARBOUR RESULTS

A problem with the computer software programme used to compile results in the Strathfield Car Radios Pittwater-to-Coffs Harbour race has resulted in a change in the overall results. In fact, the results were finally compiled by KEN MORRISON, the Hawaiian-based chairman of the Sydney-to-Hobart race jury using his laptop programme.

While Gazebo Hotel owner and recently named Ocean Racer of the Year, SYD FISCHER, remains the overall IMS winner with his Farr-50, Ragamuffin, the revised results saw the Mumm-36, Sea, skippered by advertising agency boss STEVE KULMAR, dropped from second to third place.
The Pittwater J-35, Soundtrack, skippered by MIKE PERJANIK, went up to second place, dropping ANDREW STRACHAN's Ninety Seven out of a placing.

Both Ragamuffin and Ninety Seven were casualties of the southerly buster on the first afternoon of the Sydney-to-Hobart, Ragamuffin ripping her best mainsail to shreds and Ninety Seven being damaged first of all in a starting line collision and then ripping her mainsail trying to rejoin the fleet.

Fischer is reported to have told his crew when they got back to the harbour that he wasn't going to waste all the preparation, so he dug out an old mainsail, lodged a late entry with the Royal Prince Alfred Yacht Club and headed north the following day.
Ragamuffin took line honours, first on IMS overall and first under PHS handicaps.
BIG LASER FLEET FOR NATIONALS IN ADELAIDE

There will be a star-studded fleet in Adelaide this weekend for the Australian championships for the Olympic singlehanded class, the Laser, with more than 250 competitors from all states and overseas.
Heading the fleet will be Olympian MICHAEL BLACKBURN, who finished fourth overall at Savannah after winning the final race.

Also competing will be the 1994 Laser world champion and New Zealand Olympic team member NICK BURFOOT. SIMON SMART, another Kiwi and the world youth champion, will also compete, as will Australia's youth bronze medallist MATTHEW VON BIBRA from Brisbane.

A fleet of 250 is expected for the open division and 100 in the Laser Radial division, where the smaller sail area will ensure a large contingent of women and youth sailors, including current world champion and seven-times Australian women's champion, JACQUELINE ELLIS from Lake Macquarie.
ATTENTION TURNS TO ONE-DESIGN CLASSES
The yacht scene now turns to international and national one-design classes with a series of world championships throughout Australia over the next couple of weeks.

Adelaide's Royal South Australian Yacht Club will host the International Etchells keelboat national titles starting tomorrow, while the Royal Yacht Club of Tasmania has the traditional Cadet dinghy Australian championships being followed by the Prince Philip Cup for that traditional keelboat class, the International Dragons.
Among the competitors in the Dragons will be GORDON INGATE, who has competed in every Prince Philip Cup since its inception.

In Melbourne, the Port Phillip Regatta, sponsored this year by Hewlett Packard, will run from Saturday week and has attracted an outstanding line-up of ocean racing keelboats as well as traditional boats and training yachts.
* Peter Campbell is the editor of Offshore Yachting magazine.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800.
